title: The Uganda Licence Mo Ibrahim's Clients Would Not Touch
dek: In 1998 Mo Ibrahim could not persuade the phone companies he advised to bid for free African licences, so his consultancy became an operator.

story.event: Turning from consultant to operator after clients refused African licences such as Uganda's
story.summary: In 1998 Mo Ibrahim, who ran the British mobile-network consultancy MSI, failed to persuade the telephone companies he advised to bid for cheap or free African licences, including one in Uganda, and set up MSI Cellular Investments (later Celtel) to do it himself. Starting from a minority stake in Celtel Uganda and licences in Malawi, Zambia, Sierra Leone and Congo-Brazzaville, it was built on equity under a board rule against bribes, and was sold to Kuwait's MTC for $3.4 billion in 2005.
paragraphs: In 1998 Mo Ibrahim was running MSI, the mobile-network consultancy he had founded in Britain in 1989 after working as an engineer at British Telecom. By his own account he kept asking his clients, the world's big phone companies, why they ignored Africa, where some licences cost nothing. Uganda's government, he recalled, had a free licence waiting for a bidder. When he urged a friend on the board of an American phone company to take it, the friend asked whether he had heard of Idi Amin. Amin, Ibrahim replied, had left long ago.

He had never run a network; he later called himself "a techie engineer". His consultancy, which he put at 800 staff, earned steady fees, and his clients thought Africa too risky. "So I decided I had to do it myself," he wrote. MSI Cellular Investments began that year with five employees and the consultancy's money. Its starting point, says the investment firm Ibrahim later founded, was a minority stake in Celtel Uganda, the country's first mobile network, launched in 1995 and serving about 5,000 subscribers. It also took licences in Malawi, Zambia, Sierra Leone and Congo-Brazzaville.

Banks, he said later, would not lend, so it was built on equity: $16 million in the first year, by his count, with the Commonwealth Development Corporation investing from 1998 and the International Finance Corporation approving a $10 million stake in 1999. His board included Vodafone's first chief executive and Salim Ahmed Salim, a former Tanzanian prime minister; Ibrahim, though majority owner, kept one seat. The board agreed, he recalled, that "this company will not pay one dollar in bribes". It bid only in open tenders, and any payment over $30,000 needed the full board's approval.

At first the operator was a sideline. By March 2000, a trade paper reported, it had sold its Indian interests and had working networks in five African countries, Uganda, Zambia and Malawi among them. That April Marconi announced it was buying MSI, and Ibrahim turned to the operator full-time: "we transformed ourselves from a service company to an operator," he said. In March 2005, as the renamed Celtel prepared to list its shares, Kuwait's MTC bought it for $3.4 billion; it had more than five million customers in 13 countries.

quote.text: They who imagine truth in untruth, and see untruth in truth, never arrive at truth, but follow vain desires.
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: Ibrahim's friend held a picture of Uganda that was two decades out of date. The verse names what such a picture costs: it does not leave people standing still but sends them after the wrong things, as his clients paid millions for licences elsewhere and left the free ones untouched.

reflection: Ibrahim's friend was not foolish. He was working from a picture that had once been true and had never been looked at again. Most people carry a few of those, about a place, a colleague, a family member, or about themselves: what you can manage after a long week, or what people around you will or will not pay for.

In the end Ibrahim stopped trying to argue his clients round. He looked at the place as it was, decided, and set his rules before anyone tested them. Checking an old picture against the present is slow, plain work, and it goes better on a rested morning than at the end of a tiring day.
invitation: Pick one belief about your work that you formed more than a year ago. Ask one person who sees it from outside whether it still matches what they see, and listen to the answer without defending it.

cross_checks.claim: Ibrahim founded MSI in 1989 and set up the African operator (MSI Cellular Investments, later Celtel) in 1998.
A telecom contact refused to take up a Ugandan licence because he believed Idi Amin still ran the country, and Ibrahim decided to do it himself.
The company started from a minority stake in Celtel Uganda, which launched in 1995 as Uganda's first mobile operator.
Banks would not lend, so the company was built on equity, including CDC from 1998 and an IFC equity stake approved in 1999.
The board agreed the company would pay no bribes and that payments over $30,000 needed board approval.
By March 2000 it had working networks in five African countries including Uganda, Zambia and Malawi, after licences taken from 1998.
Marconi agreed to buy MSI in 2000.
In March 2005 MTC bought Celtel for $3.4 billion; it had more than five million customers in 13 countries.

research_notes: Uganda and dates: Ibrahim dates the Idi Amin conversation to 1998 (HBR 2012; CFR 2013, 'That was in 1998'), but the IFC's 1999 disclosure says CelTel launched in Uganda in 1995 as the first cellular operator, with the MSI cellular holding company owning 42% and Vodafone 37% by 1999, and Satya Capital (Ibrahim's investment firm) says Celtel began with a minority holding in that Ugandan licence. When and how MSI acquired the Uganda stake is not documented in the sources, so the story does not date it and does not claim the free licence Ibrahim was offered became Celtel's. HBR's own timeline lists the 1998 licences as Malawi, Zambia, Sierra Leone and Congo; 'Congo' is read as Congo-Brazzaville because the DRC licence is listed for 1999 and RCR (2000) names the Republic of Congo. Country/region: the decision was taken by a London-based consultant and the first licences spanned several countries; Uganda/East Africa is used because the pivotal conversation and Celtel's starting holding both concern Uganda. The contact: HBR calls him a senior telecom executive whom Ibrahim pulled aside; CFR says a friend on the board of a Baby Bell, at a dinner in London; the story says a friend on the board of a large American phone company and leaves out the dinner. Years since Amin: Ibrahim said 'years ago' (HBR) and '20 years ago' (CFR); CNBC wrote 15 years; Amin fell in 1979, so the story says 'long ago' in the narrative and 'two decades' only in the connection. Funding source: HBR says the consulting firm provided the initial investment; at CFR Ibrahim said the money came from selling MSI (about $900 million), which happened in 2000, two years after the start. The story follows HBR. Marconi price: HBR says more than $900 million and CFR 'about $900 million', while Agence Europe's April 2000 bulletin reported USD 618 million (and a workforce of 600, against Ibrahim's 800 in 1998); the story gives no price and attributes the 800 figure to Ibrahim. MSI Cellular was not only African at first: RCR (March 2000) reports it had just sold wireless operations in India and was about to sell those in Hong Kong; the story mentions only the completed Indian sale. CDC: ITWeb (2005) says Actis, formerly part of the Commonwealth Development Corporation, began investing in Celtel seven years earlier, which the story renders as CDC investing from 1998. Customers and staff at sale: HBR gives 5.2 million managed customers and 5,000 staff in 2004; ITWeb (March 2005) more than five million customers; Satya over six million subscribers and 3,000 direct employees by 2005; Wikipedia's 24 million is a later figure. The story uses ITWeb's 'more than five million' and leaves out staff. Sale value: $3.4 billion (HBR, ITWeb, Satya, CNBC); Monocle gives EUR 2.48 billion, and the MTC deal was structured as 85% upfront with an option on the remaining 15%; the story uses $3.4 billion. HBR also says Celtel declined opportunities in Guinea and Angola over corruption, but RCR (2000) listed Guinea among planned networks, so the story leaves both countries out. Quotation 'this company will not pay one dollar in bribes' and 'we transformed ourselves from a service company to an operator' are from the CFR transcript; 'a techie engineer' and 'So I decided I had to do it myself' from HBR. This is a different episode, country and company from the existing Strive Masiyiwa/Econet licence-fight edition. The repeat screen flags samir-ibrahim-sunculture-rainmaker-pay-as-you-grow-2017 as same-founder only because of the shared surname; Samir Ibrahim of SunCulture is a different person and company, and the screen lets this edition through without changes.
